axes.title: Evidence: attention, curiosity and activation

citation.title: A Cognitive Process Theory of Writing

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Writing is a recursive, goal-directed process in which planning, translating ideas into text and reviewing interleave, rather than a straight line from first line to last.

rule.if: A long or strategic piece is requested.
rule.then: Work in internal stages: diagnose the barrier, build the argument, draft, then review critically against the brief.

studies.practice: Name the central objection the piece must overcome before drafting the first paragraph.
limits: A short operational request (microcopy, one headline) does not need the full staged process.
Staging is the order of your own work. It does not mean asking the user to approve each stage, and the requested format still wins.
caveats: A descriptive model of how writers work. It does not show that staging raises conversion.

citation.title: Cognitive Load During Problem Solving: Effects on Learning

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Working memory is limited, and unnecessary processing demands compete with the processing that builds understanding.

rule.if: The offer or concept is complex.
rule.then: Give each paragraph one main idea, group related items and use short lists, so the reader spends effort on the message and not on decoding the page.

studies.practice: At the decision point, remove competing elements such as secondary links and parallel jargon.
limits: Never cut price, guarantee, cancellation or legal terms in the name of simplicity.
caveats: The "4 to 7 elements" figure in popular summaries is not from this paper: Miller (1956) gave about seven and Cowan (2001) argues for about four chunks.
The terms extraneous and germane load come from later cognitive-load work, not from this 1988 paper.
The research concerns learning from problem solving; applying it to landing pages is an extrapolation.

related.citation: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87-114.

citation.authors: Kintsch, W., & van Dijk, T. A.
citation.title: Toward a Model of Text Comprehension and Production

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Readers understand text by linking sentence-level propositions to a global topic structure. When the link breaks, they must reread or lose the thread.

rule.if: The topic or argument shifts between paragraphs.
rule.then: Add a plain logical connective that ties the previous point to the next one.

studies.practice: State how the next paragraph follows from the last (a consequence, an obstacle, a contrast) instead of jumping topic.
limits: Do not use inflated connectives that nobody says aloud.
caveats: A comprehension model; it does not rank connective styles by persuasiveness.
studies.example: That works until [specific obstacle]. Here is where it breaks: [mechanism].

citation.title: Consequences of Erudite Vernacular Utilized Irrespective of Necessity: Problems with Using Long Words Needlessly

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Needlessly complex wording lowered readers' ratings of the author's intelligence and of the text, rather than raising them.

rule.if: A simple, common word carries the full meaning of a more elaborate one.
rule.then: Use the simple word.

studies.practice: Replace abstract business phrasing with the concrete thing that actually happens for the reader.
limits: Keep technical terms when the audience needs exact terminology (medicine, software, tax law).
caveats: The finding concerns needless complexity, not technical precision.
studies.example: Instead of "leverage operational synergies", write "remove repetitive tasks so your team ships sooner".

citation.authors: McNamara, D. S., Kintsch, E., Songer, N. B., & Kintsch, W.
citation.title: Are Good Texts Always Better? Interactions of Text Coherence, Prior Knowledge, and Levels of Understanding in Learning from Text

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Highly coherent, explicit text helps readers with low prior knowledge, while readers with high prior knowledge can do better with less explicit text that makes them work.

rule.if: The audience is a beginner (low awareness) versus a senior specialist.
rule.then: For beginners, explain premises step by step. For specialists, skip the basics and go to mechanism, specifications and metrics.

studies.practice: Selling to a technical buyer: do not define the category; show the numbers and constraints they evaluate.
limits: Never assume prior knowledge the brief does not support. When unsure, start at an intermediate level.
caveats: Measured learning from science texts, not purchase decisions.

citation.authors: Sadoski, M., Goetz, E. T., & Rodriguez, M.
citation.title: Engaging Texts: Effects of Concreteness on Comprehensibility, Interest, and Recall in Four Text Types

citation_status.note: bibliographic record matched through a web search of secondary indexes; full text not read

studies.finding: Across four text types, concreteness was strongly associated with comprehensibility and interest, consistent with dual coding of verbal and imagery information.

rule.if: You state an abstract benefit such as comfort, speed or savings.
rule.then: Attach an observable, checkable anchor to it.

studies.practice: Pair each abstract claim with a specification or a familiar comparison taken from the brief.
limits: The anchor must be a true specification of the product. Do not invent a comparison that distorts it.
caveats: Some of the supplied base's numbers, such as "twice as fast", are not supported by anything we could verify and are not used here.
Part of the evidence is correlational.
studies.example: [Abstract benefit]: [verified measurement], about the size or weight of [familiar object].

citation.title: The Psychology of Curiosity: A Review and Reinterpretation

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Curiosity arises when people notice a gap between what they know and what they want to know, so it needs some existing knowledge to open the gap.

rule.if: You write a headline, an opening or an email subject line.
rule.then: State something the reader already recognizes, then expose a specific piece of missing information.

studies.practice: Contrast a familiar situation with an unexplained detail that the body then resolves.
limits: No empty clickbait. The promised information must be delivered substantially in the body.
caveats: A theoretical account of curiosity, not a measured effect on click-through.
studies.example: [Familiar situation]. [Specific missing piece] is explained in the next section.

citation.title: What Makes Online Content Viral?

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Sharing is driven by physiological arousal: high-arousal emotions such as awe and anger increased sharing, while low-arousal emotions such as sadness did not.

rule.if: The goal is organic sharing or engagement.
rule.then: Build the angle around awe or a justified moral objection that the facts support.

studies.practice: Prefer a factual, energetic point of view to a lukewarm tip.
limits: Never use fear or outrage to spread panic or misinformation, especially in health and finance.
Invented urgency or fear violates the project integrity rules whatever the study says.
caveats: The data came from news articles, not advertising; transfer to sales copy is not shown.

citation.authors: Petty, R. E., & Cacioppo, J. T.
citation.title: The Elaboration Likelihood Model of Persuasion

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: People process messages by a central route (scrutinizing arguments) when motivated and able, and by a peripheral route (cues) otherwise.

rule.if: The decision is high-involvement or high-risk, versus a low-involvement impulse choice.
rule.then: High involvement: lead with argument quality, evidence and causal logic. Low involvement: lead with clarity, ease of action and credible social proof.

studies.practice: Judge involvement from the audience and the decision, not only from the price tag.
limits: Credibility basics matter on both routes. Do not assume polish compensates for a weak argument.
caveats: The routes are not mutually exclusive in practice; involvement varies by person.

citation.title: The Influence of Source Credibility on Communication Effectiveness

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Messages from sources seen as expert and trustworthy produced more immediate opinion change than the same message from a low-credibility source.

rule.if: You have verifiable authority, such as real experience, certification or documented results.
rule.then: Say it early, next to the claim it supports, and tie it to the reader's outcome.

studies.practice: Use only credentials the brief contains and that you can source.
limits: No vanity self-promotion. Authority matters only as a guarantee for the customer's result.
Do not rely on a "sleeper effect" to recover a weak source later.
caveats: The sleeper effect is not robust: a meta-analysis found it only under specific conditions.

related.citation: Kumkale, G. T., & Albarracin, D. (2004). The sleeper effect in persuasion: A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 130(1), 143-172.

citation.authors: Cialdini, R. B., Reno, R. R., & Kallgren, C. A.
citation.title: A Focus Theory of Normative Conduct: Recycling the Concept of Norms to Reduce Littering in Public Places
citation.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

citation_status.note: bibliographic data and main finding matched in secondary indexes; the supplied claim that descriptive norms beat injunctive norms is not what the paper reports

studies.finding: Norms influence behavior when they are made salient: descriptive norms (what others do) and injunctive norms (what is approved) each changed littering when attention was on that type. A littered setting led to more littering.

rule.if: You ask the reader to adopt or buy.
rule.then: Show what comparable people actually do, using real and sourced data.

studies.practice: State the real adoption of people like the reader, with the source and the date.
limits: Do not highlight an undesired behavior as common ("many customers pay late"); that can normalize it.
Never use an invented count. Use only figures in the brief, and obtain consent for testimonials.
caveats: A follow-up reported injunctive norm manipulations were more robust across situations than descriptive ones, and a 2021 replication of parts of the work was mixed. Do not state that descriptive norms are generally stronger.

related.citation: Reno, R. R., Cialdini, R. B., & Kallgren, C. A. (1993). The transsituational influence of social norms. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 64(1), 104-112.

citation.title: The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Choices changed when the same outcomes were described as gains or as losses.

rule.if: The audience is comfortable with the status quo, or is risk-averse.
rule.then: Make the cost of inaction concrete for the first, and frame the offer as protecting something the reader already has for the second.

studies.practice: Quantify what the current approach costs using the reader's own numbers or a sourced figure.
limits: No invented losses and no alarmism. The cost of waiting must be a supported fact.
Health, finance and other regulated categories need claim and permission review before any loss framing.
caveats: The commonly quoted loss-to-gain weight of about 2 to 2.5 is not from this paper. It comes from a 1992 estimate based on a small student sample, and loss aversion has since been argued to be over-generalized.
studies.example: Right now [current method] costs you [verified amount or time] each [period].

related.citation: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1992). Advances in prospect theory: Cumulative representation of uncertainty. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 5(4), 297-323.
Gal, D., & Rucker, D. D. (2018). The loss of loss aversion: Will it loom larger than its gain? Journal of Consumer Psychology, 28(3), 497-516.

citation.title: Mental Accounting and Consumer Choice

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: People code spending into separate mental accounts, and how a cost is categorized changes how acceptable it feels.

rule.if: The absolute price feels high.
rule.then: Relate it to a recurring unit or to a comparable spend the buyer already makes, when the comparison is true.

studies.practice: Show the per-period figure only together with the total, billing cadence and cancellation terms.
limits: The total price, recurrence and cancellation terms stay visible wherever a per-day or per-month figure appears.
The comparison must be realistic and causal for this buyer.
caveats: The "pennies-a-day" tactic is from Gourville (1998), whose results depend on which comparison standard the reframing triggers. It is not a guaranteed lever.

related.citation: Gourville, J. T. (1998). Pennies-a-day: The effect of temporal reframing on transaction evaluation. Journal of Consumer Research, 24(4), 395-408.

citation.authors: Ariely, D., Loewenstein, G., & Prelec, D.
citation.title: "Coherent Arbitrariness": Stable Demand Curves Without Stable Preferences

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Willingness to pay was strongly influenced by arbitrary initial anchors while remaining coherent across related goods.

rule.if: You are about to introduce a price.
rule.then: Establish a legitimate reference first, such as the documented cost of the current alternative.

studies.practice: Place the real cost of the incumbent method or competing option before the offer price, in the same view.
limits: The reference must be a documented fact in the brief, not an invented number.
An implausible anchor reduces trust. The actual price and terms must stay plainly visible.
caveats: Anchoring magnitudes vary across studies. Using competitor cost as the anchor is a practical extension, not what this paper tested.
studies.example: [Documented cost of the current alternative], versus [offer price and terms].

citation.title: The Nature of Psychological Reactance Revisited: A Meta-Analytic Review

citation_status.note: the supplied base gave a different title and pages 108-137; corrected from the publisher record found through a web search

studies.finding: Messages perceived as threatening freedom of choice arouse reactance (anger and negative thoughts), which works against compliance.

rule.if: You write a firm call to action or an assertive invitation.
rule.then: Avoid coercive absolutes and keep the choice explicitly with the reader, without making the action vague.

studies.practice: Replace "you must" with a clear action that names the condition under which it makes sense.
limits: Do not weaken the CTA until it is hesitant or unclear.
caveats: The "but you are free" technique is not from this paper. A re-examination of its literature found a medium pooled effect but no clear effect in the lowest-risk-of-bias studies, so treat it as something to test, not a default.
studies.example: If this fits your situation, [specific action].

related.citation: Fillon et al., re-examination of the "but you are free" technique, Meta-Psychology (found via search summary; confirm the reference before quoting).

citation.title: Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: People tend to seek, interpret and remember evidence in ways that favor beliefs they already hold.

rule.if: You are correcting a common belief of the audience.
rule.then: Acknowledge what is reasonable about the belief before presenting the contrary evidence.

studies.practice: Say under which conditions the old belief was correct, then show what changed, with a source.
limits: Never mock the reader for the old belief.
Acknowledging a belief must not endorse a false claim.
caveats: A review of the bias itself. "Agree first, then redirect" is a practitioner tactic that is not tested by this review.
studies.example: That was a reasonable conclusion when [condition]. [Verified change] means [new situation].

citation.authors: Freedman, J. L., & Fraser, S. C.
citation.title: Compliance Without Pressure: The Foot-in-the-Door Technique
citation.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Agreeing to a small first request raised compliance with a larger later request in the original studies.

rule.if: Friction for a direct purchase or proposal is high.
rule.then: Offer a low-friction first step such as a trial, a short diagnostic or a sample.

studies.practice: Make the first step genuinely useful and clearly described, with exact terms.
limits: Do not insert a pointless step for someone ready to buy now.
Do not promise free access, no commitment or a refund unless the brief confirms it.
caveats: Later meta-analyses found small effects, and a direct replication reported that the original magnitude was not reproduced. Expect much less than the 1966 results.

related.citation: Dillard, J. P., Hunter, J. E., & Burgoon, M. (1984). Sequential-request persuasive strategies: Meta-analysis of foot-in-the-door and door-in-the-face. Human Communication Research, 10(4), 461-488.

citation.authors: Green, M. C., & Brock, T. C.
citation.title: The Role of Transportation in the Persuasiveness of Public Narrative
citation.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Readers who become absorbed in a story adopt more story-consistent beliefs and notice fewer flaws.

rule.if: The audience is skeptical of dry claims.
rule.then: Use a real case with a protagonist who faced the same obstacle, resolved with verifiable facts.

studies.practice: Open with the situation the reader recognizes, not with the product.
limits: The story must be true, sourced and approved for use. A fabricated case is a hard failure.
Reduced counter-arguing is a reason for more care, not for exploiting the effect.
Skip long stories in fast-decision channels such as SMS.
caveats: Studies used narrative texts, mostly outside advertising.

citation.title: Meta-Analytic Evidence for the Persuasive Effect of Narratives on Beliefs, Attitudes, Intentions, and Behaviors

citation_status.note: bibliographic record matched through a web search of secondary indexes; full text not read

studies.finding: Narratives had small-to-moderate positive effects on beliefs, attitudes, intentions and behaviors.

rule.if: You build an institutional or long-term retention piece.
rule.then: Center the story on the customer's situation and outcome, with the brand as the tool.

studies.practice: Make the user the protagonist; keep the company as the facilitator.
limits: Do not use long narratives in fast-decision channels.
caveats: The supplied base said the effects are "highly durable" and depend on value identification with the protagonist. We could not confirm either claim, so neither is used.
Fictionality results were reported as mixed; for commercial copy use real stories only.

citation.title: Attitudinal Effects of Mere Exposure
citation.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

citation_status.note: bibliographic data taken from the supplied base; not independently checked

studies.finding: Repeated exposure to a neutral stimulus tended to increase liking for it.

rule.if: You design an email sequence, a campaign or a nurture flow.
rule.then: Keep terms, positioning line and voice consistent across touchpoints.

studies.practice: Reuse the same name for the mechanism and the same promise wording, and vary format and angle.
limits: Repetition without variation causes fatigue.
Consistency must not carry over a claim that has since been found unsupported.
caveats: Effects are modest and depend on stimulus and number of exposures.

citation.title: Message Design Choices Don't Make Much Difference to Persuasiveness and Can't Be Counted On: Not Even When Moderating Conditions Are Specified

citation_status.note: the supplied base gave Frontiers in Communication 6, 686734 and a different title; corrected from the publisher record found through a web search

studies.finding: Reviewing 30 message variations across 1,149 studies, mean effects were small (median about r = .10) and the prediction intervals included zero, even when moderating conditions were specified.

rule.if: You choose a copy strategy or structure.
rule.then: Justify the choice by the diagnosed audience barrier, and propose a test when a decision depends on it.

studies.practice: Describe why a version addresses a specific barrier. Never claim it converts because it follows a named formula.
limits: Theory generates hypotheses. Measured results in the real market decide.
caveats: The review covers message variations in persuasion research, not only advertising.
studies.example: This version addresses [diagnosed barrier] with [element]; test it against [alternative] using [metric] and [guardrail].
studies.topic: Small and variable effects of message design
